Edge cases / interview checks: Boxing creates wrapper objects and can add allocation overhead. Prefer primitive streams for large numeric pipelines.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) boxed result space

Q329Stream

Implement pagination with skip and limit

Return one page from a list using a zero-based page number and a positive page size.

Complexity: O(n) traversal in the worst case; O(pageSize) result space
Sample input / test data
List<String> names = Arrays.asList("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G");
int page = 1, pageSize = 3;
Expected output
[D, E, F]
Java 8 solution
List<String> result = names.stream()
    .skip((long) page * pageSize)
    .limit(pageSize)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<String> result = new ArrayList<String>();
int start = page * pageSize;
for (int i=start; i<names.size() && result.size()<pageSize; i++) result.add(names.get(i));
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: skip discards the first page * pageSize elements, then limit takes at most pageSize values. Casting to long avoids overflow in the multiplication.

Edge cases / interview checks: Validate page >= 0 and pageSize > 0. For very large or unordered sources, offset pagination may be inefficient or have unstable ordering.

Complexity: O(n) traversal in the worst case; O(pageSize) result space

Q330Stream

Sort objects with a multi-key comparator

Sort words by length ascending, then alphabetically for equal lengths.

Complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) result space
Sample input / test data
List<String> words = Arrays.asList("pear", "fig", "kiwi", "apple", "plum");
Expected output
[fig, kiwi, plum, apple, pear]
Java 8 solution
List<String> result = words.stream()
    .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length).thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder()))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<String> result = new ArrayList<String>(words);
Collections.sort(result, new Comparator<String>() {
    public int compare(String a, String b) {
        int byLength = Integer.compare(a.length(), b.length());
        return byLength != 0 ? byLength : a.compareTo(b);
    }
});
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: comparingInt avoids manual comparator arithmetic. thenComparing supplies a tie-breaker and makes the ordering deterministic.

Edge cases / interview checks: Do not compare numbers by subtraction because overflow can produce an invalid comparator result. Define null handling explicitly when values can be null.

Complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) result space

Q331Stream

Compare findFirst and findAny safely

Find the first matching value in an ordered stream and understand why findAny is not a fixed positional choice.

Complexity: O(n) worst-case time; O(1) auxiliary space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> numbers = Arrays.asList(2, 6, 9, 12);
int threshold = 5;
Expected output
findFirst=6; findAny is any matching value (6, 9 or 12)
Java 8 solution
Integer first = numbers.stream().filter(n -> n > threshold).findFirst().orElse(-1);
Integer any = numbers.parallelStream().filter(n -> n > threshold).findAny().orElse(-1);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Integer first = null, any = null;
for (Integer n : numbers) if (n > threshold) { first = n; any = n; break; }
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: findFirst respects encounter order when one exists. findAny allows the implementation to return any matching element and can be useful in parallel processing.

Edge cases / interview checks: Do not assert that parallel findAny always returns a particular value. Both methods return Optional and are empty when no element matches.

Complexity: O(n) worst-case time; O(1) auxiliary space

Q332Stream

Use match operations with empty streams

Evaluate anyMatch, allMatch and noneMatch and account for their results on an empty stream.

Complexity: O(n) worst-case time; O(1) auxiliary space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> positive = Arrays.asList(2, 4, 6);
List<Integer> empty = Collections.emptyList();
Expected output
positive: any=true, all=true, none=true; empty: any=false, all=true, none=true
Java 8 solution
boolean any = positive.stream().anyMatch(n -> n > 5);
boolean all = positive.stream().allMatch(n -> n > 0);
boolean none = positive.stream().noneMatch(n -> n < 0);
boolean emptyAny = empty.stream().anyMatch(n -> n > 0);
boolean emptyAll = empty.stream().allMatch(n -> n > 0);
boolean emptyNone = empty.stream().noneMatch(n -> n > 0);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
boolean any=false, all=true, none=true;
for (Integer n : positive) { if (n>5) any=true; if (n<=0) all=false; if (n>0) none=false; }
boolean emptyAny=false, emptyAll=true, emptyNone=true;
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: The methods are short-circuiting terminal operations. allMatch and noneMatch are true for an empty stream because no counterexample exists; anyMatch is false.

Edge cases / interview checks: This empty-input behavior is easy to miss in validation code. Decide whether an empty collection should be accepted by the business rule.

Complexity: O(n) worst-case time; O(1) auxiliary space

Q333Stream

Concatenate two streams in encounter order

Combine two streams into one sequence without creating an intermediate list.

Complexity: O(n+m) time; O(n+m) result space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> first = Arrays.asList(1, 2);
List<Integer> second = Arrays.asList(3, 4);
Expected output
[1, 2, 3, 4]
Java 8 solution
List<Integer> result = Stream.concat(first.stream(), second.stream()).collect(Collectors.toList());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<Integer>(first);
result.addAll(second);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Stream.concat creates a stream that emits all elements from the first stream followed by all elements from the second.

Edge cases / interview checks: Both input streams are consumed by the concatenated stream. Close resource-backed streams when required; do not reuse either input stream afterwards.

Complexity: O(n+m) time; O(n+m) result space

Q334Stream

Short-circuit a pipeline with limit and findFirst

Find the first value above a threshold while counting how many elements the sequential filter examines.

Complexity: O(k) time for the position k of the first match; O(1) auxiliary space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> numbers = Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6);
int threshold = 3;
Expected output
result=4; examined=4
Java 8 solution
AtomicInteger examined = new AtomicInteger();
Integer result = numbers.stream()
    .filter(n -> { examined.incrementAndGet(); return n > threshold; })
    .findFirst().orElse(-1);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
int examined = 0, result = -1;
for (Integer n : numbers) { examined++; if (n > threshold) { result=n; break; } }
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: findFirst can stop traversal as soon as the first match is found. This is a short-circuiting terminal operation; later elements are not evaluated.

Edge cases / interview checks: The examined count is deterministic here because the stream is sequential and the source is ordered. Parallel execution may evaluate more elements.

Complexity: O(k) time for the position k of the first match; O(1) auxiliary space

Q335Stream

Recognize and handle stream reuse errors

Demonstrate that a stream cannot be operated on twice and handle the exception deliberately.

Complexity: O(n) for count; O(1) additional space
Sample input / test data
Stream<Integer> stream = Stream.of(1, 2, 3);
Expected output
firstCount=3; secondOperation=IllegalStateException
Java 8 solution
long firstCount = stream.count();
String secondOperation;
try { stream.findFirst(); secondOperation = "unexpected success"; }
catch (IllegalStateException ex) { secondOperation = ex.getClass().getSimpleName(); }
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<Integer> values = Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3);
int firstCount = values.size();
String secondOperation = "A collection can be traversed again";
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: A Stream is a one-use traversal pipeline, not a data container. Keep the collection or a Supplier<Stream<T>> when a fresh traversal is needed.

Edge cases / interview checks: Do not catch this exception as normal control flow. Create a new stream from its source for each terminal operation.

Complexity: O(n) for count; O(1) additional space

Q336Stream

Avoid modifying the stream source during traversal

Create a transformed result without mutating the source collection while its stream is running.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> source = new ArrayList<Integer>(Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3));
Expected output
source=[1, 2, 3]; doubled=[2, 4, 6]
Java 8 solution
List<Integer> doubled = source.stream().map(n -> n * 2).collect(Collectors.toList());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<Integer> doubled = new ArrayList<Integer>();
for (Integer n : source) doubled.add(n * 2);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Stream behavioral parameters should be non-interfering: they should not modify the source while the pipeline is operating on it. Build a separate result instead.

Edge cases / interview checks: Mutating an ArrayList from inside its stream pipeline can cause ConcurrentModificationException or unpredictable behavior. If mutation is required, use an explicit, well-defined loop or a separate collection.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space

Q337Stream

Preserve encounter order with forEachOrdered

Process a parallel stream while preserving the source encounter order at the terminal action.

Complexity: O(n) work; O(n) result space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> numbers = Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3, 4, 5);
Expected output
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
Java 8 solution
List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<Integer>();
numbers.parallelStream().map(n -> n).forEachOrdered(result::add);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<Integer>();
for (Integer n : numbers) result.add(n);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: forEachOrdered preserves encounter order even when upstream work is parallel. It can reduce the performance benefit of parallel execution because ordered emission requires coordination.

Edge cases / interview checks: Do not use an ordinary ArrayList with parallel forEach because concurrent writes are unsafe. forEachOrdered performs terminal actions in order.

Complexity: O(n) work; O(n) result space

Q338Stream

Flatten arrays nested inside a collection

Flatten a list of integer arrays into one list using flatMap and Arrays.stream.

Complexity: O(total elements) time; O(total elements) result space
Sample input / test data
List<int[]> groups = Arrays.asList(new int[]{1, 2}, new int[]{3}, new int[]{4, 5});
Expected output
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
Java 8 solution
List<Integer> flat = groups.stream()
    .flatMapToInt(Arrays::stream)
    .boxed().collect(Collectors.toList());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<Integer> flat = new ArrayList<Integer>();
for (int[] group : groups) for (int value : group) flat.add(value);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: flatMapToInt maps each int[] to an IntStream and flattens those streams into one IntStream. boxed() is used only because the requested result is List<Integer>.

Edge cases / interview checks: Null arrays require filtering or validation before Arrays.stream is called. The output preserves the nested arrays’ encounter order.

Complexity: O(total elements) time; O(total elements) result space

Q339Stream

Filter distinct objects by a derived key

Keep the first spelling of each name case-insensitively using a concurrent set as the seen-key store.

Complexity: O(n) expected time; O(k) key space
Sample input / test data
List<String> names = Arrays.asList("Akash", "AKASH", "Neha", "neha", "Ravi");
Expected output
[Akash, Neha, Ravi]
Java 8 solution
Set<String> seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
List<String> unique = names.stream()
    .filter(name -> seen.add(name.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Set<String> seen = new HashSet<String>();
List<String> unique = new ArrayList<String>();
for (String name : names) {
    String key = name.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);
    if (seen.add(key)) unique.add(name);
}
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Stream.distinct uses equals/hashCode on the full element. For distinct-by-key, track the normalized key explicitly. The concurrent set makes the membership operation safe if the stream is later made parallel, though which duplicate wins can then be nondeterministic.

Edge cases / interview checks: This predicate is stateful. Prefer sequential execution when “first encountered spelling wins” is part of the contract. Filter null names before lowercasing.

Complexity: O(n) expected time; O(k) key space

Q340Stream

Sort nullable strings safely

Sort strings alphabetically while placing null values last.

Complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) result space
Sample input / test data
List<String> names = Arrays.asList("Neha", null, "Amit", "Ravi");
Expected output
[Amit, Neha, Ravi, null]
Java 8 solution
List<String> sorted = names.stream()
    .sorted(Comparator.nullsLast(Comparator.naturalOrder()))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<String> sorted = new ArrayList<String>(names);
Collections.sort(sorted, new Comparator<String>() {
    public int compare(String a, String b) {
        if (a == null) return b == null ? 0 : 1;
        if (b == null) return -1;
        return a.compareTo(b);
    }
});
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Comparator.nullsLast wraps a comparator and defines where null references belong. It avoids calling compareTo on null.

Edge cases / interview checks: Choose nullsFirst or nullsLast according to the business requirement. This handles null references, not blank strings.

Complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) result space

Q341Stream

Reduce values with and without an identity

Calculate a sum with an identity and a maximum without an identity.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> numbers = Arrays.asList(3, 7, 2);
List<Integer> empty = Collections.emptyList();
Expected output
sum=12; max=Optional[7]; emptyMax=Optional.empty
Java 8 solution
int sum = numbers.stream().reduce(0, Integer::sum);
Optional<Integer> max = numbers.stream().reduce(Integer::max);
Optional<Integer> emptyMax = empty.stream().reduce(Integer::max);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
int sum=0; for (Integer n : numbers) sum += n;
Integer max=null; for (Integer n : numbers) if (max==null || n>max) max=n;
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: An identity value is returned for an empty stream. The overload without an identity returns Optional because there may be no result.

Edge cases / interview checks: The accumulator must be associative for safe parallel reduction. The identity must be neutral for the operation; using an incorrect identity changes the answer.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space

Q342Stream

Use collect for mutable reduction instead of reduce

Collect names into an ArrayList using the mutable collector pattern.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space
Sample input / test data
List<String> names = Arrays.asList("Amit", "Neha", "Ravi");
Expected output
[Amit, Neha, Ravi]
Java 8 solution
List<String> result = names.stream().collect(ArrayList::new, ArrayList::add, ArrayList::addAll);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<String> result = new ArrayList<String>();
for (String name : names) result.add(name);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: The three-argument collect overload provides a supplier, accumulator and combiner for mutable reduction. It is the right abstraction for building a mutable container.

Edge cases / interview checks: Do not use reduce with a mutable ArrayList identity; shared mutable reduction can break parallel execution. Use collect for mutable containers.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space

Q343Stream

Count Unicode code points instead of UTF-16 char units

Compare String.length() with codePointCount for a string containing a supplementary Unicode character.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space
Sample input / test data
String text = "A😀B";
Expected output
utf16Units=4; codePoints=3
Java 8 solution
long codePoints = text.codePoints().count();
int utf16Units = text.length();
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
int codePoints = text.codePointCount(0, text.length());
int utf16Units = text.length();
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: String.length() counts UTF-16 code units. codePoints() exposes Unicode code points, which is more appropriate for many character-counting tasks.

Edge cases / interview checks: A code point is not necessarily a user-perceived grapheme cluster; combining marks and emoji sequences may contain several code points.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space

Q344Stream

Calculate numeric summary statistics

Obtain count, sum, min, average and max from one traversal of an integer stream.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> scores = Arrays.asList(70, 80, 90);
Expected output
count=3; sum=240; min=70; average=80.0; max=90
Java 8 solution
IntSummaryStatistics stats = scores.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).summaryStatistics();
long count = stats.getCount();
long sum = stats.getSum();
int min = stats.getMin();
double average = stats.getAverage();
int max = stats.getMax();
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
long sum=0; int min=Integer.MAX_VALUE, max=Integer.MIN_VALUE;
for (Integer score : scores) { sum+=score; min=Math.min(min,score); max=Math.max(max,score); }
double average = scores.isEmpty() ? 0.0 : (double)sum/scores.size();
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: summaryStatistics computes several aggregates in one pass. It avoids repeatedly traversing the source for each metric.

Edge cases / interview checks: For an empty stream count and sum are zero; min and max use sentinel values and average is NaN. Check getCount() before relying on min/max.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space

Q345Stream

Find the top N distinct numbers

Return the three largest distinct values in descending order.

Complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> numbers = Arrays.asList(5, 9, 1, 9, 7, 5, 8);
int n = 3;
Expected output
[9, 8, 7]
Java 8 solution
List<Integer> top = numbers.stream().distinct()
    .sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()).limit(n).collect(Collectors.toList());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Set<Integer> unique = new TreeSet<Integer>(Collections.reverseOrder());
unique.addAll(numbers);
List<Integer> top = new ArrayList<Integer>();
for (Integer value : unique) { if (top.size()==n) break; top.add(value); }
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: distinct must run before limit so repeated high values do not occupy several positions. reverseOrder produces descending order.

Edge cases / interview checks: If n is negative reject it; n=0 returns an empty list. Sorting all distinct values costs O(k log k); a heap can be preferable for very large inputs and small n.

Complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) space

Q346Stream

Convert an Optional result into a Java 8 stream pipeline

Turn an Optional value into zero or one stream elements without using Optional.stream(), which was added after Java 8.

Complexity: O(1) time and space per Optional
Sample input / test data
Optional<String> present = Optional.of("java");
Optional<String> absent = Optional.empty();
Expected output
present=[JAVA]; absent=[]
Java 8 solution
List<String> a = present.map(String::toUpperCase).map(Collections::singletonList).orElseGet(Collections::emptyList);
List<String> b = absent.map(String::toUpperCase).map(Collections::singletonList).orElseGet(Collections::emptyList);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String present = "java";
String absent = null;
List<String> a = new ArrayList<String>();
if (present != null) a.add(present.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT));
List<String> b = new ArrayList<String>();
if (absent != null) b.add(absent.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT));
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Java 8 Optional does not have stream(). Map the value to a singleton list and use an empty list as the fallback when integrating with collection-based code.

Edge cases / interview checks: Do not copy examples using Optional.stream() into a Java 8 project; that method arrived in Java 9. Avoid calling get() without checking presence.

Complexity: O(1) time and space per Optional

Q347Stream

Build a stream with Stream.Builder

Assemble a stream dynamically with builder.add() and then consume it once.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space
Sample input / test data
Stream.Builder<String> builder = Stream.builder();
builder.add("Java").add("Streams").add("Optional");
Expected output
[Java, Streams, Optional]
Java 8 solution
List<String> topics = builder.build().collect(Collectors.toList());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<String> topics = new ArrayList<String>();
topics.add("Java"); topics.add("Streams"); topics.add("Optional");
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Stream.Builder is useful when values are accumulated conditionally before the stream is created. build() finalizes the builder and returns the stream.

Edge cases / interview checks: Do not call build() more than once or add more elements after build(). The resulting stream is still single-use.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space

Q348Stream

Use mapToLong and mapToDouble for numeric transformations

Parse decimal strings into a DoubleStream and calculate total and average values.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space
Sample input / test data
List<String> prices = Arrays.asList("10.5", "20.25", "4.25");
Expected output
total=35.0; average=11.6666666667 (approximately)
Java 8 solution
double total = prices.stream().mapToDouble(Double::parseDouble).sum();
OptionalDouble average = prices.stream().mapToDouble(Double::parseDouble).average();
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
double total=0.0;
for (String price : prices) total += Double.parseDouble(price);
double average = prices.isEmpty() ? 0.0 : total / prices.size();
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: mapToDouble converts each input into a primitive double value; mapToLong does the same for long values. Primitive streams provide numeric terminal operations without wrapper objects.

Edge cases / interview checks: Parsing can throw NumberFormatException. Use BigDecimal rather than double for exact decimal financial calculations.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space

Q349Stream

Use peek for pipeline debugging without business side effects

Inspect elements as they pass through a pipeline, then filter even numbers.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(k) result space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> values = Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3, 4);
Expected output
peek:1; peek:2; peek:3; peek:4; result=[2, 4]
Java 8 solution
List<Integer> result = values.stream()
    .peek(n -> System.out.println("peek:" + n))
    .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<Integer>();
for (Integer n : values) {
    System.out.println("peek:" + n);
    if (n%2==0) result.add(n);
}
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: peek attaches an observation action to elements as they pass a pipeline. It is intended mainly for debugging and inspection; collect triggers the traversal.

Edge cases / interview checks: Do not rely on peek for required business side effects. Optimizations or short-circuiting operations may mean not every element is observed.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(k) result space

Q350Stream

Distinguish stateless and stateful intermediate operations

Filter positive values and sort them, showing a stateless operation followed by a stateful operation.

Complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> values = Arrays.asList(5, -1, 3, 2, -4);
Expected output
[2, 3, 5]
Java 8 solution
List<Integer> result = values.stream()
    .filter(n -> n > 0)  // stateless intermediate operation
    .sorted()             // stateful intermediate operation
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<Integer>();
for (Integer n : values) if (n>0) result.add(n);
Collections.sort(result);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: filter and map are stateless because each element can be processed independently. sorted and distinct are stateful because they may need information about multiple elements or the entire input.

Edge cases / interview checks: Stateful operations can require buffering and more memory. Consider their cost in large or parallel pipelines.

Complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) space

Q351Stream

Compare sequential and parallel stream results safely

Calculate the same sum sequentially and in parallel, checking correctness rather than assuming parallel is faster.

Complexity: O(n) total work; parallel speedup depends on workload and hardware
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> values = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10000).boxed().collect(Collectors.toList());
Expected output
sequential=50005000; parallel=50005000; equal=true
Java 8 solution
long sequential = values.stream().mapToLong(Integer::longValue).sum();
long parallel = values.parallelStream().mapToLong(Integer::longValue).sum();
boolean equal = sequential == parallel;
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<Integer> values = new ArrayList<Integer>();
for (int i=1; i<=10000; i++) values.add(i);
long sequential=0;
for (Integer n : values) sequential += n;
long parallelEquivalent = sequential; // Java 7 has no parallel Stream API.
boolean equal = sequential == parallelEquivalent;
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Java 8 can run the sum using stream() and parallelStream(). Java 7 has no Stream or parallelStream API, so its equivalent is a sequential loop; this confirms the expected result but does not simulate parallel execution.

Edge cases / interview checks: Parallel is not automatically faster: splitting, coordination and combining have costs. Avoid shared mutable state and blocking operations; benchmark realistic workloads.

Complexity: O(n) total work; parallel speedup depends on workload and hardware

Additional Interview-Critical Problems (Q438–Q439)

Q438Interview extension

Use a parallel stream reduction with an associative operation

Calculate the sum of a list safely with parallel reduction using an identity and associative accumulator.

Complexity: O(n) total work; parallel execution overhead applies
Sample input / test data
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
Expected output
15
Java 8 – complete program
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class ParallelStreamReductionJava8 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Integer> values=Arrays.asList(1,2,3,4,5);
        int sum=values.parallelStream().reduce(0,(left,right)->left+right);
        System.out.println(sum);
    }
}
Java 7-compatible equivalent – complete program
import java.util.*;

public class ParallelStreamReductionJava7 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Integer> values=Arrays.asList(1,2,3,4,5);
        int sum=0;
        for(Integer value:values) sum+=value;
        System.out.println(sum);
    }
}
Interview notes and follow-up

Approach: Identify the core data structure or API operation, preserve the required ordering and define how duplicates, missing values and exceptional cases should behave.

Edge cases: Test empty input, one element, duplicate values and boundary conditions where applicable.

Interview follow-up: Why must a parallel reduce operation use an associative accumulator?

Q439Interview extension

Close an I/O-backed stream with try-with-resources

Read lines from a file using Files.lines and ensure the stream is closed after processing.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) additional memory for counting
Sample input / test data
File lines: Java, Spring, Kafka
Expected output
3
Java 8 – complete program
import java.io.*;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class CloseIoStreamJava8 {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Path path = Files.createTempFile("technologies", ".txt");
        try {
            Files.write(path, Arrays.asList("Java", "Spring", "Kafka"), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
            try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {
                System.out.println(lines.count());
            }
        } finally {
            Files.deleteIfExists(path);
        }
    }
}
Java 7-compatible equivalent – complete program
import java.io.*;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.*;

public class CloseIoStreamJava7 {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Path path = Files.createTempFile("technologies", ".txt");
        try {
            Files.write(path, Arrays.asList("Java", "Spring", "Kafka"), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
            BufferedReader reader = Files.newBufferedReader(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
            try {
                int count = 0;
                while (reader.readLine() != null) count++;
                System.out.println(count);
            } finally {
                reader.close();
            }
        } finally {
            Files.deleteIfExists(path);
        }
    }
}
Interview notes and follow-up

Approach: Identify the core data structure or API operation, preserve the required ordering and define how duplicates, missing values and exceptional cases should behave.

Edge cases: Test empty input, one element, duplicate values and boundary conditions where applicable.

Interview follow-up: Why should I/O-backed streams be closed even after a terminal operation?

Chapter 14 – Collectors: Deep-Dive Coding (30 questions)

Q352Collector

Choose toList, toSet, LinkedHashSet and TreeSet collectors

Collect the same stream into list, insertion-ordered set and sorted set results.

Complexity: O(n log n) for TreeSet; O(n) for list/hash set
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> numbers = Arrays.asList(3, 1, 2, 1, 3);
Expected output
list=[3, 1, 2, 1, 3]; linked=[3, 1, 2]; sorted=[1, 2, 3]
Java 8 solution
List<Integer> list = numbers.stream().collect(Collectors.toList());
Set<Integer> linked = numbers.stream().collect(Collectors.toCollection(LinkedHashSet::new));
Set<Integer> sorted = numbers.stream().collect(Collectors.toCollection(TreeSet::new));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<Integer>(numbers);
Set<Integer> linked = new LinkedHashSet<Integer>(numbers);
Set<Integer> sorted = new TreeSet<Integer>(numbers);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: toList preserves encounter order but does not promise a specific concrete List type. toCollection lets you request a specific collection implementation.

Edge cases / interview checks: toSet does not promise iteration order. TreeSet requires mutually comparable elements and rejects null with natural ordering.

Complexity: O(n log n) for TreeSet; O(n) for list/hash set

Q353Collector

Build a map with toMap and unique keys

Convert a list of words into a map from each word to its length.

Complexity: O(n) expected time; O(n) map space
Sample input / test data
List<String> words = Arrays.asList("java", "stream", "optional");
Expected output
{java=4, stream=6, optional=8}
Java 8 solution
Map<String,Integer> lengths = words.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(Function.identity(), String::length));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Map<String,Integer> lengths = new LinkedHashMap<String,Integer>();
for (String word : words) lengths.put(word, word.length());
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: toMap takes a key mapper and a value mapper. Each input element contributes one key/value pair.

Edge cases / interview checks: Duplicate keys throw IllegalStateException when no merge function is supplied. Null keys/values depend on the map implementation and collector constraints.

Complexity: O(n) expected time; O(n) map space

Q354Collector

Resolve duplicate keys with a merge function

Create a word-to-total-length map while summing lengths for duplicate first-letter keys.

Complexity: O(n) expected time; O(k) map space
Sample input / test data
List<String> words = Arrays.asList("apple", "ant", "bear", "bat");
Expected output
{a=8, b=7}
Java 8 solution
Map<Character,Integer> totals = words.stream().collect(
    Collectors.toMap(w -> w.charAt(0), String::length, Integer::sum, LinkedHashMap::new));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Map<Character,Integer> totals = new LinkedHashMap<Character,Integer>();
for (String w : words) {
    char key=w.charAt(0);
    totals.put(key, totals.containsKey(key) ? totals.get(key)+w.length() : w.length());
}
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: The third toMap argument is the merge function called when two values produce the same key. The fourth argument selects the map implementation.

Edge cases / interview checks: The merge function should be associative and preferably stateless. Decide whether collisions should sum, keep first, keep last, or select a maximum.

Complexity: O(n) expected time; O(k) map space

Q355Collector

Choose a TreeMap with the toMap map supplier

Collect word lengths by word into a TreeMap so keys are displayed alphabetically.

Complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) map space
Sample input / test data
List<String> words = Arrays.asList("pear", "apple", "fig");
Expected output
{apple=5, fig=3, pear=4}
Java 8 solution
Map<String,Integer> lengths = words.stream().collect(
    Collectors.toMap(Function.identity(), String::length, (a,b) -> a, TreeMap::new));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Map<String,Integer> lengths = new TreeMap<String,Integer>();
for (String word : words) lengths.put(word, word.length());
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: The map supplier overload controls the returned map type and ordering. The merge function is still required when duplicate keys are possible.

Edge cases / interview checks: TreeMap uses key ordering and costs O(log k) per insertion. Keys must be comparable or a Comparator must be supplied.

Complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) map space

Q356Collector

Group values and count each group

Count how many words begin with each first character.

Complexity: O(n log k) time with TreeMap; O(k) map space
Sample input / test data
List<String> words = Arrays.asList("apple", "ant", "bear", "bat", "cat");
Expected output
{a=2, b=2, c=1}
Java 8 solution
Map<Character,Long> counts = words.stream().collect(
    Collectors.groupingBy(w -> w.charAt(0), TreeMap::new, Collectors.counting()));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Map<Character,Long> counts = new TreeMap<Character,Long>();
for (String word : words) {
    char key=word.charAt(0);
    counts.put(key, counts.containsKey(key) ? counts.get(key)+1L : 1L);
}
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: groupingBy classifies elements by a key and applies a downstream collector to each bucket. counting() produces Long counts.

Edge cases / interview checks: An empty input produces an empty map. If empty strings are possible, guard charAt(0) or define a separate empty-string group.

Complexity: O(n log k) time with TreeMap; O(k) map space

Q357Collector

Control grouping map type and key order

Group words by length and keep group keys sorted using a TreeMap.

Complexity: O(n log k) time; O(n) grouped result space
Sample input / test data
List<String> words = Arrays.asList("hi", "cat", "no", "java", "sun");
Expected output
{2=[hi, no], 3=[cat, sun], 4=[java]}
Java 8 solution
Map<Integer,List<String>> grouped = words.stream().collect(
    Collectors.groupingBy(String::length, TreeMap::new, Collectors.toList()));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Map<Integer,List<String>> grouped = new TreeMap<Integer,List<String>>();
for (String word : words) {
    int key=word.length();
    if (!grouped.containsKey(key)) grouped.put(key,new ArrayList<String>());
    grouped.get(key).add(word);
}
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: The three-argument groupingBy accepts a classifier, map factory and downstream collector. This gives deterministic sorted group keys.

Edge cases / interview checks: The lists within each group preserve encounter order for an ordered source. A TreeMap sorts keys, not the elements inside each list.

Complexity: O(n log k) time; O(n) grouped result space

Q358Collector

Use mapping as a downstream collector

Group words by length but store uppercase words rather than original words.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space
Sample input / test data
List<String> words = Arrays.asList("hi", "no", "java");
Expected output
{2=[HI, NO], 4=[JAVA]}
Java 8 solution
Map<Integer,List<String>> grouped = words.stream().collect(
    Collectors.groupingBy(String::length,
        Collectors.mapping(s -> s.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT), Collectors.toList())));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Map<Integer,List<String>> grouped = new HashMap<Integer,List<String>>();
for (String word : words) {
    int key=word.length();
    if (!grouped.containsKey(key)) grouped.put(key,new ArrayList<String>());
    grouped.get(key).add(word.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT));
}
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: mapping transforms each element before passing it to the downstream collector. It avoids creating an intermediate grouped list and then transforming every bucket.

Edge cases / interview checks: Use Locale.ROOT for locale-independent case conversion. Null words must be filtered or handled before length()/toUpperCase().

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space

Q359Collector

Calculate sum, average and statistics per group

Group integer amounts by category and compute count, sum, min, average and max for each group.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(k) statistics space
Sample input / test data
List<String> categories = Arrays.asList("A", "A", "B", "B", "B");
List<Integer> amounts = Arrays.asList(10, 20, 5, 15, 25);
Expected output
A: count=2 sum=30 min=10 avg=15.0 max=20; B: count=3 sum=45 min=5 avg=15.0 max=25
Java 8 solution
Map<String,IntSummaryStatistics> stats = IntStream.range(0, categories.size()).boxed()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(categories::get,
        Collectors.mapping(amounts::get, Collectors.summarizingInt(Integer::intValue))));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Map<String,List<Integer>> groups = new LinkedHashMap<String,List<Integer>>();
for (int i=0;i<categories.size();i++) {
    String key=categories.get(i);
    if (!groups.containsKey(key)) groups.put(key,new ArrayList<Integer>());
    groups.get(key).add(amounts.get(i));
}
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: summarizingInt returns IntSummaryStatistics with count, sum, min, average and max. mapping adapts the values before the downstream collector receives them.

Edge cases / interview checks: This sample uses parallel lists only to keep the example small; production code should model each category/amount pair as one object to avoid index mismatches.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(k) statistics space

Q360Collector

Partition with downstream counting

Count even and odd numbers with one partitioningBy collector.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) result space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> numbers = Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3, 4, 6);
Expected output
{false=2, true=3}
Java 8 solution
Map<Boolean,Long> counts = numbers.stream().collect(
    Collectors.partitioningBy(n -> n % 2 == 0, Collectors.counting()));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
long even=0, odd=0;
for (Integer n : numbers) { if (n%2==0) even++; else odd++; }
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: partitioningBy divides elements into exactly two Boolean groups and applies a downstream collector to each group. Unlike groupingBy, both keys are present.

Edge cases / interview checks: The keys are true for even and false for odd in this example. Empty partitions have a count of zero.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) result space

Q361Collector

Partition and map each bucket to names

Partition words by length threshold and store uppercase values in each bucket.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space
Sample input / test data
List<String> words = Arrays.asList("go", "java", "stream", "api");
int threshold = 3;
Expected output
{false=[GO, API], true=[JAVA, STREAM]}
Java 8 solution
Map<Boolean,List<String>> result = words.stream().collect(
    Collectors.partitioningBy(w -> w.length() > threshold,
        Collectors.mapping(w -> w.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT), Collectors.toList())));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Map<Boolean,List<String>> result = new LinkedHashMap<Boolean,List<String>>();
result.put(Boolean.TRUE,new ArrayList<String>()); result.put(Boolean.FALSE,new ArrayList<String>());
for (String w : words) result.get(w.length()>threshold).add(w.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT));
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: partitioningBy supplies the classification; mapping transforms each element inside each bucket. The Boolean keys are true and false.

Edge cases / interview checks: The predicate in this example is length > threshold, so length 3 belongs to false. Check the exact comparison in boundary tests.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space

Q362Collector

Group data at two levels

Group strings first by length and then by their first character.

Complexity: O(n log k) map insertion cost; O(n) result space
Sample input / test data
List<String> words = Arrays.asList("hi", "hat", "hen", "no", "net");
Expected output
{2={h=[hi], n=[no]}, 3={h=[hat, hen], n=[net]}}
Java 8 solution
Map<Integer,Map<Character,List<String>>> result = words.stream().collect(
    Collectors.groupingBy(String::length, TreeMap::new,
        Collectors.groupingBy(w -> w.charAt(0), TreeMap::new, Collectors.toList())));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Map<Integer,Map<Character,List<String>>> result = new TreeMap<Integer,Map<Character,List<String>>>();
for (String w : words) {
    int len=w.length(); char first=w.charAt(0);
    if (!result.containsKey(len)) result.put(len,new TreeMap<Character,List<String>>());
    Map<Character,List<String>> inner=result.get(len);
    if (!inner.containsKey(first)) inner.put(first,new ArrayList<String>());
    inner.get(first).add(w);
}
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Nest groupingBy collectors to create a hierarchy. Each grouping level has its own classifier, optional map factory and downstream collector.

Edge cases / interview checks: The maps use TreeMap for predictable key order. Empty strings need special handling before charAt(0).

Complexity: O(n log k) map insertion cost; O(n) result space

Q363Collector

Sort each grouped list with collectingAndThen

Group words by length and sort each resulting list alphabetically before returning the map.

Complexity: O(n log n) overall for per-group sorting; O(n) result space
Sample input / test data
List<String> words = Arrays.asList("pear", "fig", "plum", "apple");
Expected output
{3=[fig], 4=[pear, plum], 5=[apple]}
Java 8 solution
Map<Integer,List<String>> result = words.stream().collect(
    Collectors.groupingBy(String::length, TreeMap::new,
        Collectors.collectingAndThen(Collectors.toList(),
            list -> { Collections.sort(list); return list; })));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Map<Integer,List<String>> result = new TreeMap<Integer,List<String>>();
for (String w : words) {
    int key=w.length();
    if (!result.containsKey(key)) result.put(key,new ArrayList<String>());
    result.get(key).add(w);
}
for (List<String> list : result.values()) Collections.sort(list);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: collectingAndThen applies a finishing transformation after the downstream collector finishes. It is useful when each completed group needs post-processing.

Edge cases / interview checks: The finisher sorts each list in place. If the caller needs immutable values, wrap the list with Collections.unmodifiableList after sorting.

Complexity: O(n log n) overall for per-group sorting; O(n) result space

Q364Collector

Return an unmodifiable collected list in Java 8

Collect values and expose a read-only list using collectingAndThen and Collections.unmodifiableList.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space
Sample input / test data
List<String> words = Arrays.asList("java", "streams");
Expected output
[java, streams]; adding an item throws UnsupportedOperationException
Java 8 solution
List<String> readOnly = words.stream().collect(
    Collectors.collectingAndThen(Collectors.toList(), Collections::unmodifiableList));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<String> mutable = new ArrayList<String>(words);
List<String> readOnly = Collections.unmodifiableList(mutable);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: The downstream collector creates a list; the finisher wraps it in a read-only view. This is still a view of the collected list, which is no longer directly exposed for mutation.

Edge cases / interview checks: Collections.unmodifiableList is a view, not a deeply immutable copy. If mutable references are stored in the list, those objects can still change.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space

Q365Collector

Reduce values inside groupingBy

Group words by their first character and calculate the total character count in each group.

Complexity: O(n log k) time; O(k) result space
Sample input / test data
List<String> words = Arrays.asList("ant", "apple", "bat", "ball");
Expected output
{a=8, b=7}
Java 8 solution
Map<Character,Integer> totals = words.stream().collect(
    Collectors.groupingBy(w -> w.charAt(0), TreeMap::new,
        Collectors.reducing(0, String::length, Integer::sum)));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Map<Character,Integer> totals = new TreeMap<Character,Integer>();
for (String w : words) { char k=w.charAt(0); totals.put(k,totals.containsKey(k)?totals.get(k)+w.length():w.length()); }
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: reducing(identity, mapper, op) maps each word to its length, then combines the mapped values within each group.

Edge cases / interview checks: The identity must be neutral for Integer.sum. For non-associative operations or incorrect identities, parallel results can be wrong.

Complexity: O(n log k) time; O(k) result space

Q366Collector

Join transformed elements with delimiter, prefix and suffix

Convert words to uppercase and join them into one formatted string.

Complexity: O(total characters) time; O(total characters) result space
Sample input / test data
List<String> words = Arrays.asList("java", "streams", "api");
Expected output
[JAVA | STREAMS | API]
Java 8 solution
String result = words.stream()
    .map(w -> w.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT))
    .collect(Collectors.joining(" | ", "[", "]"));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
StringBuilder result = new StringBuilder("[");
for (int i=0;i<words.size();i++) {
    if (i>0) result.append(" | ");
    result.append(words.get(i).toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT));
}
result.append("]");
String output=result.toString();
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: joining concatenates CharSequence values. The overload accepts a delimiter, prefix and suffix, which is useful for formatted output.

Edge cases / interview checks: An empty input produces the prefix plus suffix. Avoid repeated string concatenation in loops; StringBuilder is the Java 7 alternative.

Complexity: O(total characters) time; O(total characters) result space

Q367Collector

Use maxBy and minBy downstream collectors

Find the longest and shortest word in one collection using Optional results.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space
Sample input / test data
List<String> words = Arrays.asList("java", "stream", "api");
Expected output
longest=Optional[stream]; shortest=Optional[api]
Java 8 solution
Optional<String> longest = words.stream().collect(Collectors.maxBy(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)));
Optional<String> shortest = words.stream().collect(Collectors.minBy(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String longest=null, shortest=null;
for (String w : words) {
    if (longest==null || w.length()>longest.length()) longest=w;
    if (shortest==null || w.length()<shortest.length()) shortest=w;
}
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: maxBy and minBy return Optional because an empty input has no maximum or minimum. A comparator defines the ordering used for selection.

Edge cases / interview checks: Tie behavior follows encounter/reduction behavior; add a secondary comparator when deterministic tie-breaking is required.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space

Q368Collector

Use groupingByConcurrent for concurrent grouping

Group a large list of numbers by parity using the concurrent grouping collector.

Complexity: O(n) expected work; O(n) result space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> numbers = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 8).boxed().collect(Collectors.toList());
Expected output
odd=[1, 3, 5, 7]; even=[2, 4, 6, 8] (group order is not guaranteed)
Java 8 solution
ConcurrentMap<Boolean,List<Integer>> grouped = numbers.parallelStream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingByConcurrent(n -> n % 2 == 0));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Map<Boolean,List<Integer>> grouped = new HashMap<Boolean,List<Integer>>();
for (Integer n : numbers) {
    boolean even=n%2==0;
    if (!grouped.containsKey(even)) grouped.put(even,new ArrayList<Integer>());
    grouped.get(even).add(n);
}
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: groupingByConcurrent uses a ConcurrentMap and is suitable for concurrent reduction when encounter order is not required. It can help parallel grouping for appropriate workloads.

Edge cases / interview checks: Do not rely on map/list iteration order. Concurrent collection is not automatically faster; benchmark with realistic data and avoid shared downstream side effects.

Complexity: O(n) expected work; O(n) result space

Q369Collector

Build a custom average Collector with supplier, accumulator, combiner and finisher

Create a reusable Collector<Integer, long[], Double> that calculates an average.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) accumulator space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> values = Arrays.asList(10, 20, 30);
Expected output
20.0
Java 8 solution
Collector<Integer,long[],Double> averageCollector = Collector.of(
    () -> new long[2],
    (a, value) -> { a[0]++; a[1] += value; },
    (left, right) -> { left[0] += right[0]; left[1] += right[1]; return left; },
    a -> a[0] == 0 ? 0.0 : (double) a[1] / a[0]);
double average = values.stream().collect(averageCollector);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
long count=0, sum=0;
for (Integer value : values) { count++; sum += value; }
double average = count==0 ? 0.0 : (double)sum/count;
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: supplier creates the mutable accumulator; accumulator incorporates one element; combiner merges partial accumulators; finisher converts the accumulator into the final result.

Edge cases / interview checks: The combiner is essential for parallel reduction and must merge partial states correctly. This simple implementation returns 0.0 for empty input; OptionalDouble may be a better API contract.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) accumulator space

Q370Collector

Build a custom Collector for a delimited string

Create a Collector that joins strings using a StringBuilder accumulator and a combiner.

Complexity: O(total characters) time; O(total characters) result space
Sample input / test data
List<String> values = Arrays.asList("A", "B", "C");
Expected output
A,B,C
Java 8 solution
Collector<String,StringBuilder,String> csvCollector = Collector.of(
    StringBuilder::new,
    (builder, value) -> { if (builder.length()>0) builder.append(","); builder.append(value); },
    (left, right) -> { if (left.length()>0 && right.length()>0) left.append(","); left.append(right); return left; },
    StringBuilder::toString);
String csv = values.stream().collect(csvCollector);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
StringBuilder csv = new StringBuilder();
for (String value : values) { if (csv.length()>0) csv.append(","); csv.append(value); }
String result = csv.toString();
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: This collector shows how a mutable accumulator can be combined. The combiner must insert the delimiter between non-empty partial results.

Edge cases / interview checks: For production CSV, escaping commas, quotes and line breaks is required. Do not declare the collector CONCURRENT because StringBuilder is not thread-safe.

Complexity: O(total characters) time; O(total characters) result space

Q371Collector

Apply a downstream collector to nested partitions

Partition numbers by even/odd and then group each partition by remainder modulo three.

Complexity: O(n log k) time; O(n) result space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> numbers = Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6);
Expected output
{false={0=[3], 1=[1], 2=[5]}, true={0=[6], 1=[4], 2=[2]}}
Java 8 solution
Map<Boolean,Map<Integer,List<Integer>>> result = numbers.stream().collect(
    Collectors.partitioningBy(n -> n % 2 == 0,
        Collectors.groupingBy(n -> n % 3, TreeMap::new, Collectors.toList())));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Map<Boolean,Map<Integer,List<Integer>>> result = new LinkedHashMap<Boolean,Map<Integer,List<Integer>>>();
result.put(Boolean.TRUE,new TreeMap<Integer,List<Integer>>());
result.put(Boolean.FALSE,new TreeMap<Integer,List<Integer>>());
for (Integer n : numbers) {
    Map<Integer,List<Integer>> bucket=result.get(n%2==0);
    int key=n%3;
    if (!bucket.containsKey(key)) bucket.put(key,new ArrayList<Integer>());
    bucket.get(key).add(n);
}
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Collectors can be composed: partitioningBy is the outer classifier and groupingBy is the downstream collector. Each nested collector sees only the values in its parent bucket.

Edge cases / interview checks: The output map has both Boolean keys even if one partition is empty. This example uses non-negative inputs; modulo for negative numbers may yield negative keys.

Complexity: O(n log k) time; O(n) result space

Q372Collector

Use summarizingDouble with employee salary data

Calculate salary statistics in a single pass using the shared Employee sample dataset.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) statistics space
Sample input / test data
List<Employee> employees = sampleEmployees();
Expected output
count=5; sum=440000.0; min=60000.0; average=88000.0; max=120000.0
Java 8 solution
DoubleSummaryStatistics stats = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.summarizingDouble(Employee::getSalary));
long count = stats.getCount();
double sum = stats.getSum();
double min = stats.getMin();
double average = stats.getAverage();
double max = stats.getMax();
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
long count=0; double sum=0, min=Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY, max=Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY;
for (Employee e : employees) { count++; double s=e.getSalary(); sum+=s; min=Math.min(min,s); max=Math.max(max,s); }
double average=count==0?0.0:sum/count;
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: summarizingDouble returns count, sum, min, average and max in one collector. It is often better than separate aggregation passes.

Edge cases / interview checks: The sample employee salaries total 440000.0. For financial calculations, use BigDecimal and a defined rounding policy rather than double.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) statistics space

Q373Collector

Unwrap a grouped Optional result with collectingAndThen

For every department, return the highest-paid employee directly, or null if the group is empty.

Complexity: O(n) expected time; O(k) map space
Sample input / test data
List<Employee> employees = sampleEmployees();
Expected output
{HR=Anil, IT=Neha}
Java 8 solution
Map<String,Employee> highest = employees.stream().collect(
    Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment,
        Collectors.collectingAndThen(
            Collectors.maxBy(Comparator.comparingDouble(Employee::getSalary)),
            opt -> opt.orElse(null))));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Map<String,Employee> highest = new HashMap<String,Employee>();
for (Employee e : employees) {
    Employee old=highest.get(e.getDepartment());
    if (old==null || e.getSalary()>old.getSalary()) highest.put(e.getDepartment(),e);
}
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: maxBy returns Optional<Employee>; collectingAndThen applies a finisher to unwrap it. Keeping Optional in the map is often safer than converting absence to null.

Edge cases / interview checks: A grouping created from a non-empty input has non-empty groups, but retaining Optional is more expressive when the result can be absent. Ties need a secondary comparator if required.

Complexity: O(n) expected time; O(k) map space

Q374Collector

Collect into a PriorityQueue with toCollection

Collect values into a min-priority queue and remove them in ascending order.

Complexity: O(n log n) time for inserts and removals; O(n) queue space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> values = Arrays.asList(7, 2, 9, 1);
Expected output
poll order=[1, 2, 7, 9]
Java 8 solution
Queue<Integer> queue = values.stream().collect(Collectors.toCollection(PriorityQueue::new));
List<Integer> pollOrder = new ArrayList<Integer>();
while (!queue.isEmpty()) pollOrder.add(queue.poll());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Queue<Integer> queue = new PriorityQueue<Integer>();
queue.addAll(values);
List<Integer> pollOrder = new ArrayList<Integer>();
while (!queue.isEmpty()) pollOrder.add(queue.poll());
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: toCollection accepts a supplier for a concrete collection. PriorityQueue exposes its minimum element through peek/poll; iteration itself is not sorted.

Edge cases / interview checks: Do not print or collect the queue by iteration and assume sorted order. Repeated poll operations produce priority order and modify the queue.

Complexity: O(n log n) time for inserts and removals; O(n) queue space

Q375Collector

Choose a merge policy for latest or largest value per key

Build a map that retains the longest word for each first character; on ties, retain the first encountered word.

Complexity: O(n) expected time; O(k) map space
Sample input / test data
List<String> words = Arrays.asList("ant", "apple", "bat", "bear", "ball");
Expected output
{a=apple, b=bear}
Java 8 solution
Map<Character,String> longest = words.stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(
    w -> w.charAt(0), Function.identity(),
    (a,b) -> a.length() >= b.length() ? a : b, LinkedHashMap::new));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Map<Character,String> longest = new LinkedHashMap<Character,String>();
for (String w : words) {
    char key=w.charAt(0); String old=longest.get(key);
    if (old==null || w.length()>old.length()) longest.put(key,w);
}
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: The merge function encodes the duplicate-key business rule. Keeping the first value on equal lengths makes the tie policy explicit.

Edge cases / interview checks: If null values are possible, get() cannot distinguish absent from present-with-null; use containsKey or reject null input. Define deterministic tie-breaking for parallel streams.

Complexity: O(n) expected time; O(k) map space

Q376Collector

Compare groupingBy and partitioningBy for binary categories

Use groupingBy for a string category and partitioningBy for a Boolean predicate.

Complexity: O(n) expected time; O(n) result space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> values = Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3, 4);
Expected output
groupingBy parity={odd=[1, 3], even=[2, 4]}; partitioningBy={false=[1, 3], true=[2, 4]}
Java 8 solution
Map<String,List<Integer>> byName = values.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(n -> n%2==0 ? "even" : "odd"));
Map<Boolean,List<Integer>> byBoolean = values.stream().collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(n -> n%2==0));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Map<String,List<Integer>> byName = new HashMap<String,List<Integer>>();
Map<Boolean,List<Integer>> byBoolean = new HashMap<Boolean,List<Integer>>();
for (Integer n : values) {
    String key=n%2==0?"even":"odd";
    if (!byName.containsKey(key)) byName.put(key,new ArrayList<Integer>()); byName.get(key).add(n);
    boolean b=n%2==0; if (!byBoolean.containsKey(b)) byBoolean.put(b,new ArrayList<Integer>()); byBoolean.get(b).add(n);
}
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: groupingBy supports any key type and only creates observed groups. partitioningBy always creates true and false groups.

Edge cases / interview checks: Use the operation that matches the domain: two-way Boolean classification is naturally partitioningBy; multi-category classification is groupingBy.

Complexity: O(n) expected time; O(n) result space

Q377Collector

Avoid Java 9 and later collectors in Java 8 solutions

Create a filtered grouped result using Java 8 collectors only; filter before grouping because Collectors.filtering is not in Java 8.

Complexity: O(n log k) time; O(n) result space
Sample input / test data
List<String> words = Arrays.asList("ant", "apple", "bat", "bear");
int minLength = 4;
Expected output
{a=[apple], b=[bear]}
Java 8 solution
Map<Character,List<String>> result = words.stream()
    .filter(w -> w.length() >= minLength)
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(w -> w.charAt(0), TreeMap::new, Collectors.toList()));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Map<Character,List<String>> result = new TreeMap<Character,List<String>>();
for (String w : words) if (w.length()>=minLength) {
    char key=w.charAt(0);
    if (!result.containsKey(key)) result.put(key,new ArrayList<String>());
    result.get(key).add(w);
}
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: The Java 8-compatible approach applies filter before groupingBy. Collectors.filtering was introduced in Java 9 and must not be used in a Java 8-targeted solution.

Edge cases / interview checks: Likewise avoid Collectors.teeing (Java 12), Stream.toList() (Java 16) and Map.of() (Java 9) in Java 8 code.

Complexity: O(n log k) time; O(n) result space

Q378Collector

Use summingInt and averagingInt downstream collectors

Group words by first character and calculate the total and average word lengths in each group.

Complexity: O(n log k) time; O(k) result space
Sample input / test data
List<String> words = Arrays.asList("apple", "ant", "bear", "bat");
Expected output
sumByInitial={a=8, b=7}; averageByInitial={a=4.0, b=3.5}
Java 8 solution
Map<Character,Integer> sumByInitial = words.stream().collect(
    Collectors.groupingBy(w -> w.charAt(0), TreeMap::new, Collectors.summingInt(String::length)));
Map<Character,Double> averageByInitial = words.stream().collect(
    Collectors.groupingBy(w -> w.charAt(0), TreeMap::new, Collectors.averagingInt(String::length)));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Map<Character,Integer> sumByInitial = new TreeMap<Character,Integer>();
Map<Character,Integer> countByInitial = new TreeMap<Character,Integer>();
for (String w : words) {
    char key=w.charAt(0);
    sumByInitial.put(key,sumByInitial.containsKey(key)?sumByInitial.get(key)+w.length():w.length());
    countByInitial.put(key,countByInitial.containsKey(key)?countByInitial.get(key)+1:1);
}
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: summingInt returns an Integer total, while averagingInt returns a Double average. Both can be used as downstream collectors inside groupingBy.

Edge cases / interview checks: Use summingLong/summingDouble or averagingLong/averagingDouble for other numeric types. Define behavior for empty groups and empty strings.

Complexity: O(n log k) time; O(k) result space

Q379Collector

Inspect Collector characteristics

Create a list collector with IDENTITY_FINISH and inspect its declared characteristics.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space
Sample input / test data
Collector<Integer,List<Integer>,List<Integer>> collector = Collector.of(
    ArrayList::new, List::add,
    (left, right) -> { left.addAll(right); return left; },
    Collector.Characteristics.IDENTITY_FINISH);
Expected output
values=[1, 2, 3]; characteristics=[IDENTITY_FINISH]
Java 8 solution
List<Integer> values = Stream.of(1, 2, 3).collect(collector);
Set<Collector.Characteristics> characteristics = collector.characteristics();
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<Integer> values = Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3);
List<Integer> collected = new ArrayList<Integer>(values);
// Java 7 has no Stream Collector characteristics API.
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: IDENTITY_FINISH means the accumulator container is also the final result. CONCURRENT permits concurrent accumulation under the collector contract; UNORDERED means encounter order is not required. These characteristics are Java 8 Collector metadata and have no Java 7 API equivalent.

Edge cases / interview checks: Do not declare CONCURRENT unless the accumulator supports concurrent updates. Do not declare UNORDERED if encounter order affects the result.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space

Additional Interview-Critical Problems (Q440–Q441)

Q440Interview extension

Collect grouped results into a TreeMap

Group employee names by department while keeping department keys sorted.

Complexity: O(n log d) time; O(n) space
Sample input / test data
Sales: Ana; Engineering: Ben; Sales: Kim
Expected output
{Engineering=[Ben], Sales=[Ana, Kim]}
Java 8 – complete program
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class GroupIntoTreeMapJava8 {
    static class Employee {
        String name,department;
        Employee(String n,String d){name=n;department=d;}
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Employee> employees=Arrays.asList(
            new Employee("Ana","Sales"),new Employee("Ben","Engineering"),
            new Employee("Kim","Sales"));
        Map<String,List<String>> result=employees.stream().collect(
            Collectors.groupingBy(e -> e.department,TreeMap::new,
                Collectors.mapping(e -> e.name,Collectors.toList())));
        System.out.println(result);
    }
}
Java 7-compatible equivalent – complete program
import java.util.*;

public class GroupIntoTreeMapJava7 {
    static class Employee {
        String name,department;
        Employee(String n,String d){name=n;department=d;}
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Employee> employees=Arrays.asList(
            new Employee("Ana","Sales"),new Employee("Ben","Engineering"),
            new Employee("Kim","Sales"));
        Map<String,List<String>> result=new TreeMap<String,List<String>>();
        for(Employee e:employees) {
            if(!result.containsKey(e.department)) result.put(e.department,new ArrayList<String>());
            result.get(e.department).add(e.name);
        }
        System.out.println(result);
    }
}
Interview notes and follow-up

Approach: Identify the core data structure or API operation, preserve the required ordering and define how duplicates, missing values and exceptional cases should behave.

Edge cases: Test empty input, one element, duplicate values and boundary conditions where applicable.

Interview follow-up: When would LinkedHashMap be preferable to TreeMap for grouping?

Q441Interview extension

Build a concurrent frequency map with toConcurrentMap

Count word frequencies using a concurrent map collector.

Complexity: O(n) expected total work; concurrent contention depends on key distribution
Sample input / test data
["java", "sql", "java"]
Expected output
{java=2, sql=1}
Java 8 – complete program
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class ConcurrentWordFrequencyJava8 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> words=Arrays.asList("java","sql","java");
        ConcurrentMap<String,Integer> frequency=words.parallelStream().collect(
            Collectors.toConcurrentMap(word -> word, word -> 1, Integer::sum));
        System.out.println(new TreeMap<String,Integer>(frequency));
    }
}
Java 7-compatible equivalent – complete program
import java.util.*;

public class ConcurrentWordFrequencyJava7 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> words=Arrays.asList("java","sql","java");
        Map<String,Integer> frequency=new TreeMap<String,Integer>();
        for(String word:words) {
            Integer count=frequency.get(word);
            frequency.put(word,count==null?1:count+1);
        }
        System.out.println(frequency);
    }
}
Interview notes and follow-up

Approach: Identify the core data structure or API operation, preserve the required ordering and define how duplicates, missing values and exceptional cases should behave.

Edge cases: Test empty input, one element, duplicate values and boundary conditions where applicable.

Interview follow-up: What are the trade-offs between groupingByConcurrent and toConcurrentMap?

Chapter 15 – Optional: Deep-Dive Coding (29 questions)

Q380Optional

Create Optional with of, empty and ofNullable

Create present, empty and nullable Optional values without triggering NullPointerException.

Complexity: O(1) time and space
Sample input / test data
String value = "Java";
String nullable = null;
Expected output
present=Optional[Java]; empty=Optional.empty; fromNull=Optional.empty
Java 8 solution
Optional<String> present = Optional.of(value);
Optional<String> empty = Optional.empty();
Optional<String> fromNull = Optional.ofNullable(nullable);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String present = value;
String empty = null;
String fromNull = nullable;
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: of requires a non-null value. empty represents absence. ofNullable converts null to an empty Optional.

Edge cases / interview checks: Optional.of(null) throws NullPointerException. Use ofNullable when the source may be null.

Complexity: O(1) time and space

Q381Optional

Check presence and avoid unsafe get calls

Read a value safely and supply a fallback when the Optional is empty.

Complexity: O(1) time and space
Sample input / test data
Optional<String> value = Optional.of("Java");
Optional<String> missing = Optional.empty();
Expected output
presentValue=Java; missingValue=not-found
Java 8 solution
String presentValue = value.orElse("not-found");
String missingValue = missing.orElse("not-found");
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String value = "Java";
String missing = null;
String presentValue = value != null ? value : "not-found";
String missingValue = missing != null ? missing : "not-found";
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: The Java 8 version uses orElse. The Java 7 equivalent uses a nullable String and a conditional expression; Java 7 has no Optional class.

Edge cases / interview checks: get() throws NoSuchElementException when empty. The Java 8 API offers safer methods such as orElse, orElseGet and orElseThrow.

Complexity: O(1) time and space

Q382Optional

Use orElse for a simple default value

Return a default display name when an optional username is absent.

Complexity: O(1) time and space
Sample input / test data
Optional<String> userName = Optional.empty();
Expected output
Guest
Java 8 solution
String displayName = userName.orElse("Guest");
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String userName = null;
String displayName = userName != null ? userName : "Guest";
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: orElse takes the fallback value directly. It is concise when the fallback is cheap to create and does not have side effects.

Edge cases / interview checks: The fallback expression is evaluated before orElse is called, even when the Optional is present. Use orElseGet for lazy computation.

Complexity: O(1) time and space

Q383Optional

Distinguish eager orElse from lazy orElseGet

Count how many times a fallback supplier runs when the Optional already contains a value.

Complexity: O(1) unless fallback work is expensive
Sample input / test data
Optional<String> userName = Optional.of("Akash");
AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger();
Expected output
orElse=Akash; supplierCallsAfterOrElse=1; orElseGet=Akash; supplierCallsAfterOrElseGet=1
Java 8 solution
Supplier<String> fallback = () -> { calls.incrementAndGet(); return "Guest"; };
String first = userName.orElse(fallback.get());
int afterOrElse = calls.get();
String second = userName.orElseGet(fallback);
int afterOrElseGet = calls.get();
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String userName = "Akash";
AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger();
// Eager fallback evaluation, analogous to orElse(fallback()).
String fallbackValue = "Guest"; calls.incrementAndGet();
String first = userName != null ? userName : fallbackValue;
int afterOrElse = calls.get();
// Lazy fallback evaluation, analogous to orElseGet(supplier).
if (userName == null) calls.incrementAndGet();
String second = userName != null ? userName : "Guest";
int afterOrElseGet = calls.get();
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Both methods return Akash. orElse evaluates its argument eagerly, while orElseGet invokes the Supplier only when empty. With a present Optional the fallback supplier is not invoked by orElseGet.

Edge cases / interview checks: Include this distinction when the fallback performs database access, logging, expensive computation or other side effects. Helper method: static String loadFallback(AtomicInteger c){ c.incrementAndGet(); return "Guest"; }

Complexity: O(1) unless fallback work is expensive

Q384Optional

Throw a custom exception with orElseThrow

Return a required configuration value or throw a domain-specific exception.

Complexity: O(1) time and space
Sample input / test data
Optional<String> apiKey = Optional.empty();
Expected output
IllegalStateException: API key is missing
Java 8 solution
String key = apiKey.orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalStateException("API key is missing"));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String apiKey = null;
if (apiKey == null) throw new IllegalStateException("API key is missing");
String key = apiKey;
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Java 8 orElseThrow accepts a Supplier for the exception to throw when the Optional is empty.

Edge cases / interview checks: The supplier runs only for the empty case. Use a meaningful exception type and message that matches the method contract.

Complexity: O(1) time and space

Q385Optional

Execute an action with ifPresent

Print a username only when the Optional contains a value.

Complexity: O(1) time and space
Sample input / test data
Optional<String> userName = Optional.of("Neha");
Expected output
Welcome Neha
Java 8 solution
userName.ifPresent(name -> System.out.println("Welcome " + name));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String userName = "Neha";
if (userName != null) System.out.println("Welcome " + userName);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: ifPresent accepts a Consumer and performs an action only when the value exists. It is useful for optional side effects such as logging or notifications.

Edge cases / interview checks: ifPresent returns void. Do not use it when you need to transform and return a value; use map or flatMap instead.

Complexity: O(1) time and space

Q386Optional

Filter an Optional value with a predicate

Keep a username only when it has at least five characters.

Complexity: O(1) time and space
Sample input / test data
Optional<String> userName = Optional.of("Akash");
Expected output
Optional[Akash]
Java 8 solution
Optional<String> valid = userName.filter(name -> name.length() >= 5);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String userName = "Akash";
String valid = userName != null && userName.length() >= 5 ? userName : null;
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: filter retains the value when the predicate is true; otherwise it returns Optional.empty(). It never returns null.

Edge cases / interview checks: A null Optional reference is not the same as Optional.empty(). Ensure the Optional variable itself is not null.

Complexity: O(1) time and space

Q387Optional

Transform Optional values with map

Convert an optional username to uppercase and retain absence when there is no username.

Complexity: O(1) time and space
Sample input / test data
Optional<String> userName = Optional.of("akash");
Expected output
Optional[AKASH]
Java 8 solution
Optional<String> upper = userName.map(name -> name.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String userName = "akash";
String upper = userName == null ? null : userName.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: map applies a Function to the contained value and wraps the mapped result in Optional. It avoids manual presence checks.

Edge cases / interview checks: If the mapping function returns null, map produces Optional.empty(). Use Locale.ROOT for locale-independent case conversion.

Complexity: O(1) time and space

Q388Optional

Flatten nested Optional values with flatMap

Call a lookup method that already returns Optional and avoid creating Optional<Optional<String>>.

Complexity: O(1) expected map lookup time
Sample input / test data
Map<Integer,String> users = new HashMap<Integer,String>();
users.put(1, "Akash");
int id = 1;
Expected output
Optional[AKASH]
Java 8 solution
Optional<String> upper = Optional.of(id)
    .flatMap(key -> Optional.ofNullable(users.get(key)))    .map(name -> name.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String name = users.get(id);
String upper = name == null ? null : name.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: flatMap is used when the mapping function already returns Optional. It flattens the nested result into one Optional level.

Edge cases / interview checks: Using map with an Optional-returning function would produce Optional<Optional<T>>. Keep null handling at the boundary of the lookup.

Complexity: O(1) expected map lookup time

Q389Optional

Understand map when the mapper returns null

Map an Optional string to a nullable result and observe that the result becomes empty.

Complexity: O(1) time and space
Sample input / test data
Optional<String> input = Optional.of("java");
Expected output
Optional.empty
Java 8 solution
Optional<String> mapped = input.map(value -> (String) null);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String input = "java";
String mapped = input == null ? null : null;
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Optional.map wraps the mapper result as an Optional using ofNullable semantics. A null mapped result becomes Optional.empty.
