Edge cases / interview checks: If the mapping operation itself can fail, handle that exception separately. Optional represents absence, not every kind of error.

Complexity: O(1) time and space

Q390Optional

Navigate nested nullable properties with map

Read a nested value from a map of maps without repeated null checks.

Complexity: O(depth) time; O(1) auxiliary space
Sample input / test data
Map<String,Map<String,String>> profile = new HashMap<String,Map<String,String>>();
Map<String,String> address = new HashMap<String,String>();
address.put("city", "Hyderabad"); profile.put("Akash", address);
Expected output
Optional[Hyderabad]; missing profile=Optional.empty
Java 8 solution
Optional<String> city = Optional.ofNullable(profile.get("Akash"))
    .map(a -> a.get("city"));
Optional<String> missing = Optional.ofNullable(profile.get("Unknown"))
    .map(a -> a.get("city"));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Map<String,String> a = profile.get("Akash");
String city = a == null ? null : a.get("city");
Map<String,String> b = profile.get("Unknown");
String missing = b == null ? null : b.get("city");
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Each map() step runs only when the prior value exists. This is useful for chaining nullable getters or map lookups.

Edge cases / interview checks: Optional.ofNullable is applied at the nullable boundary. It cannot protect against a null profile reference; validate the root object too.

Complexity: O(depth) time; O(1) auxiliary space

Q391Optional

Wrap a nullable repository lookup in Optional

Create a repository-style method that returns Optional instead of returning null.

Complexity: O(1) expected map lookup time
Sample input / test data
Map<Integer,String> users = new HashMap<Integer,String>();
users.put(10, "Neha");
Expected output
find(10)=Optional[Neha]; find(99)=Optional.empty
Java 8 solution
Function<Integer,Optional<String>> findUser = id -> Optional.ofNullable(users.get(id));
Optional<String> found = findUser.apply(10);
Optional<String> missing = findUser.apply(99);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String found = users.get(10);
String missing = users.get(99);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Optional makes possible absence explicit in the return type. Callers can compose map, flatMap, filter or orElseThrow without guessing whether null means missing.

Edge cases / interview checks: Do not return a null Optional reference. Return Optional.empty() when no value exists; Optional is primarily intended as a return type.

Complexity: O(1) expected map lookup time

Q392Optional

Compose two Optional-returning service lookups

Look up a user id, then look up that user’s email only when the first lookup succeeds.

Complexity: O(1) expected lookup time per map
Sample input / test data
Map<String,Integer> ids = new HashMap<String,Integer>(); ids.put("Akash", 7);
Map<Integer,String> emails = new HashMap<Integer,String>(); emails.put(7, "akash@example.com");
Expected output
Optional[akash@example.com]; unknown user=Optional.empty
Java 8 solution
Optional<String> email = Optional.of("Akash")
    .flatMap(name -> Optional.ofNullable(ids.get(name)))
    .flatMap(id -> Optional.ofNullable(emails.get(id)));
Optional<String> missing = Optional.of("Unknown")
    .flatMap(name -> Optional.ofNullable(ids.get(name)))
    .flatMap(id -> Optional.ofNullable(emails.get(id)));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Integer id = ids.get("Akash");
String email = id == null ? null : emails.get(id);
Integer missingId = ids.get("Unknown");
String missing = missingId == null ? null : emails.get(missingId);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: flatMap chains operations that may each return an Optional. The pipeline stops at the first missing value and propagates Optional.empty().

Edge cases / interview checks: This is useful for service/repository composition, but do not hide operational failures as absence. Exceptions such as timeouts should remain distinguishable.

Complexity: O(1) expected lookup time per map

Q393Optional

Combine two Optional values with flatMap and map

Add two optional integers only when both operands are present.

Complexity: O(1) time and space
Sample input / test data
Optional<Integer> a = Optional.of(10);
Optional<Integer> b = Optional.of(20);
Expected output
Optional[30]
Java 8 solution
Optional<Integer> sum = a.flatMap(x -> b.map(y -> x + y));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Integer a = 10, b = 20;
Integer sum = a != null && b != null ? a + b : null;
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: flatMap handles the first Optional and map handles the second. The result is present only if both inputs are present.

Edge cases / interview checks: For numeric workflows where absence is common, define whether missing values should yield empty, a default, or a validation error.

Complexity: O(1) time and space

Q394Optional

Use OptionalInt for primitive search results

Find the maximum integer and avoid boxing it into Optional<Integer>.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space
Sample input / test data
int[] values = {4, 9, 2};
int[] empty = {};
Expected output
max=OptionalInt[9]; emptyMax=OptionalInt.empty
Java 8 solution
OptionalInt max = Arrays.stream(values).max();
OptionalInt emptyMax = Arrays.stream(empty).max();
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Integer max = null;
for (int value : values) if (max==null || value>max) max=value;
Integer emptyMax = null;
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: IntStream.max returns OptionalInt. Java 8 also provides OptionalLong and OptionalDouble for primitive result types.

Edge cases / interview checks: OptionalInt has isPresent(), getAsInt(), orElse() and orElseGet(IntSupplier). Do not call getAsInt() when it is empty.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space

Q395Optional

Handle Stream findFirst results with Optional methods

Find the first matching string and transform it only when it exists.

Complexity: O(n) worst-case time; O(1) auxiliary space
Sample input / test data
List<String> names = Arrays.asList("Amit", "Neha", "Ravi");
String prefix = "N";
Expected output
NEHA
Java 8 solution
String result = names.stream().filter(n -> n.startsWith(prefix))
    .findFirst().map(String::toUpperCase).orElse("NOT_FOUND");
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String result = "NOT_FOUND";
for (String name : names) if (name.startsWith(prefix)) { result=name.toUpperCase(); break; }
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: findFirst returns Optional<String>. map transforms the found value, and orElse supplies the not-found result.

Edge cases / interview checks: If no match exists, the mapping function is not called. Use orElseThrow when absence violates the method contract.

Complexity: O(n) worst-case time; O(1) auxiliary space

Q396Optional

Flatten a collection of Optional values in Java 8

Extract present values from a list of Optional<Integer> without Optional.stream(), which is unavailable in Java 8.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(k) result space
Sample input / test data
List<Optional<Integer>> values = Arrays.asList(Optional.of(1), Optional.empty(), Optional.of(3));
Expected output
[1, 3]
Java 8 solution
List<Integer> present = values.stream()
    .filter(Optional::isPresent)
    .map(Optional::get)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<Integer> values = Arrays.asList(1, null, 3);
List<Integer> present = new ArrayList<Integer>();
for (Integer value : values) if (value != null) present.add(value);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: The Java 8 version filters Optional values. Java 7 has no Optional, so the imperative equivalent uses null as the absence representation and filters null entries.

Edge cases / interview checks: Reject null Optional references in the source list or filter them explicitly. Do not use Optional.stream() because it is a Java 9 method.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(k) result space

Q397Optional

Convert Optional to zero-or-one list in Java 8

Create a list containing the Optional value when present, or an empty list when absent.

Complexity: O(1) time and space
Sample input / test data
Optional<String> value = Optional.of("Java");
Optional<String> missing = Optional.empty();
Expected output
present=[Java]; absent=[]
Java 8 solution
List<String> presentList = value.map(Collections::singletonList).orElseGet(Collections::emptyList);
List<String> absentList = missing.map(Collections::singletonList).orElseGet(Collections::emptyList);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String value = "Java";
String missing = null;
List<String> presentList = new ArrayList<String>();
if (value != null) presentList.add(value);
List<String> absentList = new ArrayList<String>();
if (missing != null) absentList.add(missing);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: map(Collections::singletonList) turns a present value into a one-element list. orElseGet supplies an empty list when absent.

Edge cases / interview checks: This pattern is a Java 8 alternative to Optional.stream(). Avoid mutating the singleton list returned by Collections.singletonList.

Complexity: O(1) time and space

Q398Optional

Chain validation rules with filter and map

Normalize an email address and keep it only when it contains exactly one @ separator.

Complexity: O(n) time relative to string length; O(1) extra space
Sample input / test data
Optional<String> email = Optional.of("  User@Example.com  ");
Expected output
Optional[user@example.com]
Java 8 solution
Optional<String> valid = email.map(String::trim)
    .filter(s -> s.indexOf("@") > 0 && s.indexOf("@") == s.lastIndexOf("@"))
    .map(s -> s.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String email = "  User@Example.com  ";
String valid = null;
if (email != null) {
    String s=email.trim();
    if (s.indexOf("@")>0 && s.indexOf("@") == s.lastIndexOf("@")) valid=s.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);
}
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: map normalizes the value, filter validates it and the final map transforms the accepted value. A failed filter becomes Optional.empty().

Edge cases / interview checks: This is only a basic format check, not complete email validation. Use a proper validation policy for production input.

Complexity: O(n) time relative to string length; O(1) extra space

Q399Optional

Use a fallback chain for configuration values

Choose the first available value from environment, file configuration and a default.

Complexity: O(1) time and space
Sample input / test data
Optional<String> environment = Optional.empty();
Optional<String> fileValue = Optional.of("staging");
Expected output
staging
Java 8 solution
String profile = environment.orElseGet(() -> fileValue.orElse("local"));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String environment = null;
String fileValue = "staging";
String profile = environment != null ? environment : (fileValue != null ? fileValue : "local");
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Nested orElseGet keeps the fallback lazy: the file value is considered only when the environment value is absent, and local is used last.

Edge cases / interview checks: Do not use a chain of Optional defaults to conceal invalid configuration. Validate the selected value after choosing the source.

Complexity: O(1) time and space

Q400Optional

Use orElseThrow after Optional validation

Find a required user and throw an exception when no matching user exists.

Complexity: O(1) expected lookup time
Sample input / test data
Map<Integer,String> users = new HashMap<Integer,String>(); users.put(1, "Neha");
int requestedId = 2;
Expected output
IllegalArgumentException: No user for id 2
Java 8 solution
String user = Optional.ofNullable(users.get(requestedId))
    .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("No user for id " + requestedId));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String user = users.get(requestedId);
if (user == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("No user for id " + requestedId);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: orElseThrow converts an absent value into a clear failure at the point where a value becomes mandatory.

Edge cases / interview checks: Use a domain-specific exception in an application. Do not catch and suppress it unless a recovery action is defined.

Complexity: O(1) expected lookup time

Q401Optional

Distinguish Optional.empty from a null Optional reference

Safely handle a nullable Optional returned by a badly behaved legacy method, then normalize the contract.

Complexity: O(1) time and space
Sample input / test data
Optional<String> legacyResult = null;
Expected output
normalized=Optional.empty; value=not-found
Java 8 solution
Optional<String> normalized = Optional.ofNullable(legacyResult).orElseGet(Optional::empty);
String value = normalized.orElse("not-found");
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String legacyValue = null;
String value = legacyValue == null ? "not-found" : legacyValue;
// In Java 7, represent absence with null; there is no Optional type.
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Optional.empty is a valid Optional object representing no value. A null Optional reference is a contract violation; normalize it only at a legacy boundary.

Edge cases / interview checks: Methods should never return null Optional. Prefer fixing the producer rather than spreading defensive wrappers throughout the application.

Complexity: O(1) time and space

Q402Optional

Use Optional.equals and hashCode for value semantics

Compare Optional values based on their contents and use them as map keys only when that behavior is desired.

Complexity: O(1) time and space
Sample input / test data
Optional<String> a = Optional.of("java");
Optional<String> b = Optional.of("java");
Optional<String> emptyA = Optional.empty();
Optional<String> emptyB = Optional.empty();
Expected output
aEqualsB=true; emptyEqualsEmpty=true
Java 8 solution
boolean same = a.equals(b);
boolean bothEmpty = emptyA.equals(emptyB);
int hash = a.hashCode();
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
boolean same = "java".equals("java");
boolean bothEmpty = true;
int hash = "java".hashCode();
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Optional implements value-based equals and hashCode based on whether a value is present and, when present, the contained value.

Edge cases / interview checks: Do not synchronize on Optional instances or rely on object identity. The API describes Optional as a value-based class.

Complexity: O(1) time and space

Q403Optional

Avoid Optional in fields and method parameters

Use a nullable input parameter and return Optional from a lookup method, rather than storing Optional as an entity field.

Complexity: O(1) expected lookup time
Sample input / test data
Map<Integer,String> users = new HashMap<Integer,String>(); users.put(5, "Ravi");
int id = 5;
Expected output
Optional[Ravi]
Java 8 solution
Function<Integer,Optional<String>> findName = key -> Optional.ofNullable(users.get(key));
Optional<String> result = findName.apply(id);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String result = users.get(id);
// A Java 7 method would return the String directly and document that null means not found.
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Optional is primarily intended to represent an optional return value. It makes absence explicit at an API boundary and composes with map/flatMap.

Edge cases / interview checks: Avoid using Optional for every field, setter parameter or collection element by default. Consider serialization, frameworks and API clarity.

Complexity: O(1) expected lookup time

Q404Optional

Use Optional with primitive numeric fallbacks

Read an optional integer result and choose a primitive default without manual boxing.

Complexity: O(n) search time; O(1) auxiliary space
Sample input / test data
OptionalInt result = IntStream.of(4, 8, 2).filter(n -> n > 10).findFirst();
Expected output
value=-1
Java 8 solution
int value = result.orElse(-1);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
int[] values = {4, 8, 2};
Integer value = null;
for (int n : values) if (n>10) { value=n; break; }
if (value==null) value=-1;
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: OptionalInt provides primitive-specific methods such as orElse and ifPresent, avoiding the wrapper Optional<Integer> for primitive results.

Edge cases / interview checks: Check whether the default value could also be a valid result; if so, keep the OptionalInt or return a separate status.

Complexity: O(n) search time; O(1) auxiliary space

Q405Optional

Return different values for present and absent cases

Build a display message using map and orElse without branching.

Complexity: O(1) time and space
Sample input / test data
Optional<String> user = Optional.of("Akash");
Optional<String> missing = Optional.empty();
Expected output
Welcome, Akash; Welcome, guest
Java 8 solution
String a = user.map(name -> "Welcome, " + name).orElse("Welcome, guest");
String b = missing.map(name -> "Welcome, " + name).orElse("Welcome, guest");
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String user = "Akash";
String missing = null;
String a = user != null ? "Welcome, " + user : "Welcome, guest";
String b = missing != null ? "Welcome, " + missing : "Welcome, guest";
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: map transforms only the present value; orElse supplies the complete message when there is no value.

Edge cases / interview checks: If building the fallback is expensive, use orElseGet. Keep formatting logic simple and avoid side effects inside map.

Complexity: O(1) time and space

Q406Optional

Use OptionalLong and OptionalDouble for primitive values

Read present and absent long/double results with primitive-specific defaults.

Complexity: O(1) time and space
Sample input / test data
OptionalLong recordId = OptionalLong.of(9001L);
OptionalDouble discount = OptionalDouble.empty();
Expected output
id=9001; discount=0.0
Java 8 solution
long id = recordId.orElse(-1L);
double discountValue = discount.orElse(0.0);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Long recordId = 9001L;
Double discount = null;
long id = recordId != null ? recordId : -1L;
double discountValue = discount != null ? discount : 0.0;
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: OptionalLong and OptionalDouble mirror OptionalInt and avoid boxing primitive results. They provide presence checks, getAsX() and fallback methods.

Edge cases / interview checks: Choose a fallback that cannot be confused with a valid value, or keep the Optional type when absence needs to remain explicit.

Complexity: O(1) time and space

Additional Interview-Critical Problems (Q442–Q443)

Q442Interview extension

Compose Optional lookups without nested Optional values

Look up a user and then their manager, returning a fallback when either lookup is absent.

Complexity: O(1) lookup operations; O(1) additional space
Sample input / test data
User has manager name: Priya
Expected output
Priya
Java 8 – complete program
import java.util.*;

public class ComposeOptionalLookupsJava8 {
    static class User {
        String manager;
        User(String manager){this.manager=manager;}
        Optional<String> getManagerName(){return Optional.ofNullable(manager);}
    }
    static Optional<User> findUser(String id) {
        return "u1".equals(id)?Optional.of(new User("Priya")):Optional.empty();
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String manager=findUser("u1")
            .flatMap(User::getManagerName).orElse("No manager");
        System.out.println(manager);
    }
}
Java 7-compatible equivalent – complete program
public class ComposeOptionalLookupsJava7 {
    static class User {
        String manager;
        User(String manager){this.manager=manager;}
    }
    static User findUser(String id) {
        return "u1".equals(id)?new User("Priya"):null;
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        User user=findUser("u1");
        String manager=(user!=null && user.manager!=null)?user.manager:"No manager";
        System.out.println(manager);
    }
}
Interview notes and follow-up

Approach: Identify the core data structure or API operation, preserve the required ordering and define how duplicates, missing values and exceptional cases should behave.

Edge cases: Test empty input, one element, duplicate values and boundary conditions where applicable.

Interview follow-up: Why is flatMap needed instead of map when the mapper already returns Optional?

Q443Interview extension

Use OptionalInt for a primitive search result

Find the first even number in an array and represent the result without boxing.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) additional space
Sample input / test data
[3, 7, 8, 10]
Expected output
8
Java 8 – complete program
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class OptionalIntSearchJava8 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] values={3,7,8,10};
        OptionalInt result=Arrays.stream(values).filter(value -> value%2==0).findFirst();
        System.out.println(result.isPresent()?result.getAsInt():"Not found");
    }
}
Java 7-compatible equivalent – complete program
public class OptionalIntSearchJava7 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] values={3,7,8,10};
        Integer result=null;
        for(int value:values) if(value%2==0) { result=value; break; }
        System.out.println(result==null?"Not found":result);
    }
}
Interview notes and follow-up

Approach: Identify the core data structure or API operation, preserve the required ordering and define how duplicates, missing values and exceptional cases should behave.

Edge cases: Test empty input, one element, duplicate values and boundary conditions where applicable.

Interview follow-up: What is the difference between Optional<Integer> and OptionalInt?

Chapter 16 – Lambda and Functional Interfaces: Deep-Dive Coding (17 questions)

Q407Functional interface

Validate two inputs with BiPredicate

Use BiPredicate<Integer,Integer> to check whether an amount is within a permitted range.

Complexity: O(1) time and space
Sample input / test data
int amount = 750;
int minimum = 100, maximum = 1000;
Expected output
valid=true
Java 8 solution
BiPredicate<Integer,Integer> atLeast = (value, min) -> value >= min;
BiPredicate<Integer,Integer> atMost = (value, max) -> value <= max;
boolean valid = atLeast.test(amount, minimum) && atMost.test(amount, maximum);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
boolean valid = amount >= minimum && amount <= maximum;
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: BiPredicate accepts two inputs and returns a boolean. Its and/or/negate methods compose validation rules.

Edge cases / interview checks: Keep predicate operations side-effect free. Ensure boundary inclusivity matches the requirement.

Complexity: O(1) time and space

Q408Functional interface

Transform two inputs with BiFunction

Combine a product name and quantity into a formatted line using BiFunction.

Complexity: O(1) time and space
Sample input / test data
String product = "Keyboard";
int quantity = 2;
Expected output
Keyboard x 2
Java 8 solution
BiFunction<String,Integer,String> line = (name, qty) -> name + " x " + qty;
String result = line.apply(product, quantity);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String result = product + " x " + quantity;
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: BiFunction<T,U,R> accepts two arguments and returns a result. It is useful for mapping two input values into one output.

Edge cases / interview checks: Use primitive-specialized interfaces when boxing costs matter. Keep formatting separate from business calculations where possible.

Complexity: O(1) time and space

Q409Functional interface

Consume two inputs with BiConsumer

Print key/value pairs from a map using BiConsumer.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space
Sample input / test data
Map<String,Integer> scores = new LinkedHashMap<String,Integer>();
scores.put("Amit", 80); scores.put("Neha", 95);
Expected output
Amit=80; Neha=95
Java 8 solution
BiConsumer<String,Integer> printer = (name, score) -> System.out.println(name + "=" + score);
scores.forEach(printer);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
for (Map.Entry<String,Integer> entry : scores.entrySet()) {
    System.out.println(entry.getKey() + "=" + entry.getValue());
}
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: BiConsumer accepts two arguments and returns no result. Map.forEach passes each key/value pair to the action.

Edge cases / interview checks: A Consumer may perform side effects, but do not mutate the map structure from inside its forEach action.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space

Q410Functional interface

Transform a value with UnaryOperator

Normalize a string using UnaryOperator<String>, where input and output types are the same.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space
Sample input / test data
String text = "  Java 8  ";
Expected output
java 8
Java 8 solution
UnaryOperator<String> normalize = s -> s.trim().toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);
String result = normalize.apply(text);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
String result = text.trim().toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: UnaryOperator<T> is a Function<T,T>. It expresses transformations that preserve the input/output type.

Edge cases / interview checks: String operations create new values because String is immutable. Define null handling before invoking trim().

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space

Q411Functional interface

Combine values with BinaryOperator

Use BinaryOperator<Integer> to find the maximum value in a reduction.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> values = Arrays.asList(4, 9, 2, 7);
Expected output
9
Java 8 solution
BinaryOperator<Integer> max = (a,b) -> a >= b ? a : b;
Integer result = values.stream().reduce(max).orElse(null);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Integer result = null;
for (Integer value : values) if (result==null || value>result) result=value;
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: BinaryOperator<T> is a BiFunction<T,T,T>. It combines two values of the same type and is commonly used with reduce.

Edge cases / interview checks: For parallel reduce, the operator should be associative. The max operation is associative; subtraction is not.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space

Q412Functional interface

Use a static method reference

Replace a lambda with a reference to an existing static parsing method.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space
Sample input / test data
List<String> values = Arrays.asList("10", "20", "30");
Expected output
[10, 20, 30]
Java 8 solution
List<Integer> numbers = values.stream().map(Integer::parseInt).collect(Collectors.toList());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<Integer> numbers = new ArrayList<Integer>();
for (String value : values) numbers.add(Integer.parseInt(value));
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: ClassName::staticMethod is a static method reference. The method signature must match the functional interface expected by map.

Edge cases / interview checks: Invalid numeric text throws NumberFormatException. Decide whether invalid values should fail the entire pipeline or be filtered/collected as errors.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space

Q413Functional interface

Use a bound instance method reference

Use a fixed String receiver as a Predicate to match one exact value.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(k) result space
Sample input / test data
List<String> values = Arrays.asList("java", "Java", "stream");
String expected = "java";
Expected output
[java]
Java 8 solution
List<String> result = values.stream().filter(expected::equals).collect(Collectors.toList());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<String> result = new ArrayList<String>();
for (String value : values) if (expected.equals(value)) result.add(value);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: expected::equals is a bound instance method reference. The receiver (expected) is fixed; each stream element is passed as the argument to equals().

Edge cases / interview checks: To filter non-empty strings, use s -> !s.isEmpty() or an appropriate predicate. Do not confuse a bound reference with String::isEmpty.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(k) result space

Q414Functional interface

Use an unbound instance method reference

Use String::toUpperCase as a Function<String,String> and transform a list.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space
Sample input / test data
List<String> words = Arrays.asList("java", "streams");
Expected output
[JAVA, STREAMS]
Java 8 solution
List<String> upper = words.stream().map(String::toUpperCase).collect(Collectors.toList());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<String> upper = new ArrayList<String>();
for (String word : words) upper.add(word.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT));
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: ClassName::instanceMethod is an unbound reference: the first argument becomes the receiver. It matches Function<String,String> for this method.

Edge cases / interview checks: For locale-independent transformations prefer an explicit lambda using Locale.ROOT; String::toUpperCase uses the default locale.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) result space

Q415Functional interface

Create objects with a constructor reference

Use a constructor reference to create StringBuilder instances from strings.

Complexity: O(total characters) time; O(n) object space
Sample input / test data
List<String> values = Arrays.asList("A", "B", "C");
Expected output
[A, B, C]
Java 8 solution
List<StringBuilder> builders = values.stream()
    .map(StringBuilder::new).collect(Collectors.toList());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<StringBuilder> builders = new ArrayList<StringBuilder>();
for (String value : values) builders.add(new StringBuilder(value));
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: ClassName::new is a constructor reference. The selected constructor must match the input argument type of the target functional interface.

Edge cases / interview checks: If several constructors are overloaded, the target functional interface type determines which constructor is selected.

Complexity: O(total characters) time; O(n) object space

Q416Functional interface

Compose Function operations with compose and andThen

Apply a function before or after another function and compare the execution order.

Complexity: O(1) time and space
Sample input / test data
Function<Integer,Integer> doubleIt = n -> n * 2;
Function<Integer,Integer> addThree = n -> n + 3;
int value = 5;
Expected output
compose=16; andThen=13
Java 8 solution
int compose = doubleIt.compose(addThree).apply(value);
int andThen = doubleIt.andThen(addThree).apply(value);
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
int compose = (value + 3) * 2;
int andThen = (value * 2) + 3;
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: compose runs the supplied function first, then the current function. andThen runs the current function first, then the supplied function.

Edge cases / interview checks: The distinction is execution order. Name composed functions clearly to prevent accidental reversal of transformations.

Complexity: O(1) time and space

Q417Functional interface

Compose Predicate with and, or and negate

Filter values that are positive and even, then invert a predicate to get odd values.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(k) result space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> values = Arrays.asList(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4);
Expected output
positiveEven=[2, 4]; odd=[-1, 1, 3]
Java 8 solution
Predicate<Integer> positive = n -> n > 0;
Predicate<Integer> even = n -> n % 2 == 0;
List<Integer> positiveEven = values.stream().filter(positive.and(even)).collect(Collectors.toList());
List<Integer> odd = values.stream().filter(even.negate()).collect(Collectors.toList());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<Integer> positiveEven = new ArrayList<Integer>(), odd = new ArrayList<Integer>();
for (Integer n : values) { if (n>0 && n%2==0) positiveEven.add(n); if (n%2!=0) odd.add(n); }
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Predicate provides default methods and(), or() and negate() to compose reusable Boolean conditions.

Edge cases / interview checks: and/or short-circuit like &&/||. Ensure predicate names describe the condition being tested.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(k) result space

Q418Functional interface

Chain Consumer actions with andThen

Run two Consumer actions in order for every name.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space
Sample input / test data
List<String> names = Arrays.asList("Amit", "Neha");
Expected output
first:Amit; second:AMIT; first:Neha; second:NEHA
Java 8 solution
Consumer<String> first = n -> System.out.println("first:" + n);
Consumer<String> second = n -> System.out.println("second:" + n.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT));
names.forEach(first.andThen(second));
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
for (String n : names) {
    System.out.println("first:" + n);
    System.out.println("second:" + n.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT));
}
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: andThen returns a Consumer that invokes the current action followed by the supplied action.

Edge cases / interview checks: If the first Consumer throws an exception, the second one is not invoked for that value. Avoid unexpected side effects in chained actions.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space

Q419Functional interface

Use primitive functional interfaces to avoid boxing

Filter and transform primitive integers using IntPredicate and IntUnaryOperator.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(k) result space
Sample input / test data
int[] values = {1, 2, 3, 4};
Expected output
[20, 40]
Java 8 solution
IntPredicate even = n -> n % 2 == 0;
IntUnaryOperator timesTen = n -> n * 10;
List<Integer> result = Arrays.stream(values).filter(even).map(timesTen).boxed().collect(Collectors.toList());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<Integer>();
for (int n : values) if (n%2==0) result.add(n*10);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: Primitive interfaces such as IntPredicate, IntUnaryOperator, IntConsumer and ToIntFunction avoid wrapper allocation in many numeric pipelines.

Edge cases / interview checks: boxed() is used only at the end because the requested output is List<Integer>. Keep IntStream if the consumer can accept primitive values.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(k) result space

Q420Functional interface

Capture effectively final variables in a lambda

Use a local threshold inside a lambda and understand the effectively-final rule.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(k) result space
Sample input / test data
List<Integer> values = Arrays.asList(10, 20, 30, 40);
int threshold = 25;
Expected output
[30, 40]
Java 8 solution
List<Integer> result = values.stream().filter(n -> n > threshold).collect(Collectors.toList());
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<Integer>();
for (Integer n : values) if (n > threshold) result.add(n);
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: A lambda can capture a local variable only when it is final or effectively final. The value cannot be reassigned after capture.

Edge cases / interview checks: If a changing counter is needed, use an appropriate mutable holder such as AtomicInteger, but avoid shared mutable state in parallel pipelines.

Complexity: O(n) time; O(k) result space

Q421Functional interface

Define a custom functional interface with default and static methods

Create a functional interface with one abstract method, plus reusable default and static methods.

Complexity: O(1) time and space
Sample input / test data
int a = 4, b = 5;
Expected output
sum=9; description=Operation; identity=0
Java 8 solution
Operation add = (x, y) -> x + y;
int sum = add.apply(a, b);
String description = add.description();
int identity = Operation.identity();
Java 7 equivalent (imperative approach)
Operation7 add = new Operation7() { public int apply(int x, int y) { return x+y; } };
int sum = add.apply(a,b);
// Java 7 interfaces cannot declare default or static methods.
Code explanation and edge cases

What the code demonstrates: The Operation interface is declared in the appendix. It has one abstract method, one default method and one static method; only the single abstract method determines whether it is lambda-compatible.

Edge cases / interview checks: The @FunctionalInterface annotation makes the compiler verify the single-abstract-method contract. Java 7 can use an anonymous class but has no interface default/static methods.

Complexity: O(1) time and space

static void reverse(int[] a,int l,int r){

Java version compatibility

  • Java 8: Streams, lambdas, method references, Optional, CompletableFuture and functional interfaces.
  • Java 7: loops, collections, anonymous classes, ExecutorService and Future.
  • Do not use Java 9+ APIs such as Stream.toList(), takeWhile(), Map.of() or Collectors.teeing() in Java 8 solutions.

Complexity conventions

Time complexity describes the core algorithm. Auxiliary space excludes the required output when stated. HashMap and HashSet operations are expected O(1), not guaranteed worst-case O(1). Sorting-based solutions are generally O(n log n). Recursive tree algorithms use O(h) stack space.

Java 8 coding API boundaries (important for interviews)

The deep-dive chapters use only Java 8 APIs. Java 9+ methods intentionally excluded: Optional.stream(), Collectors.filtering(), Collectors.flatMapping(), Collectors.teeing(), Stream.takeWhile()/dropWhile(), Stream.ofNullable(), Stream.toList(), List.of(), Set.of(), Map.of() and Optional.ifPresentOrElse().

Custom distinct-by-key helper used by advanced Stream discussions

static <T> Predicate<T> distinctByKey(Function<? super T, ?> keyExtractor) {
    Set<Object> seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
    return value -> seen.add(keyExtractor.apply(value));
}

This helper is stateful. Use a sequential stream when first-encountered ordering is required; a concurrent set makes membership checks safe but does not guarantee which duplicate survives in a parallel stream.

Functional-interface model used in the Lambda and Functional Interfaces deep-dive chapter

@FunctionalInterface
interface Operation {
    int apply(int a, int b);
    default String description() { return "Operation"; }
    static int identity() { return 0; }
}

// Java 7 equivalent interface (no default/static methods):
interface Operation7 { int apply(int a, int b); }

Additional Interview-Critical Problems (Q444–Q445)

Q444Interview extension

Compose a multi-field Comparator with thenComparing

Sort employees by department ascending, salary descending, and name ascending.

Complexity: O(n log n) time; O(log n) typical sort stack
Sample input / test data
Sales: Ana 90; Engineering: Ben 100; Sales: Kim 110
Expected output
[Ben, Kim, Ana]
Java 8 – complete program
import java.util.*;

public class ComposeComparatorJava8 {
    static class Employee {
        String name,department; int salary;
        Employee(String n,String d,int s){name=n;department=d;salary=s;}
        public String toString(){return name;}
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Employee> employees=Arrays.asList(new Employee("Ana","Sales",90),
            new Employee("Ben","Engineering",100),new Employee("Kim","Sales",110));
        employees.sort(Comparator.comparing((Employee e)->e.department)
            .thenComparing(Comparator.comparingInt((Employee e)->e.salary).reversed())
            .thenComparing(e->e.name));
        System.out.println(employees);
    }
}
Java 7-compatible equivalent – complete program
import java.util.*;

public class ComposeComparatorJava7 {
    static class Employee {
        String name,department; int salary;
        Employee(String n,String d,int s){name=n;department=d;salary=s;}
        public String toString(){return name;}
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Employee> employees=Arrays.asList(new Employee("Ana","Sales",90),
            new Employee("Ben","Engineering",100),new Employee("Kim","Sales",110));
        Collections.sort(employees,new Comparator<Employee>() {
            public int compare(Employee a,Employee b) {
                int result=a.department.compareTo(b.department);
                if(result!=0) return result;
                result=Integer.compare(b.salary,a.salary);
                if(result!=0) return result;
                return a.name.compareTo(b.name);
            }
        });
        System.out.println(employees);
    }
}
Interview notes and follow-up

Approach: Identify the core data structure or API operation, preserve the required ordering and define how duplicates, missing values and exceptional cases should behave.

Edge cases: Test empty input, one element, duplicate values and boundary conditions where applicable.

Interview follow-up: How would you make the comparator null-safe for department and name?

Q445Interview extension

Create a generic custom functional interface

Create a generic functional interface that transforms a value of type T into a value of type R.

Complexity: O(1) for this transformation; depends on converter
Sample input / test data
Input: "java"; operation: string length
Expected output
4
Java 8 – complete program
public class GenericFunctionalInterfaceJava8 {
    @FunctionalInterface
    interface Converter<T,R> { R convert(T value); }
    static <T,R> R transform(T input,Converter<T,R> converter) {
        return converter.convert(input);
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Integer length=transform("java",text -> text.length());
        System.out.println(length);
    }
}
Java 7-compatible equivalent – complete program
public class GenericFunctionalInterfaceJava7 {
    interface Converter<T,R> { R convert(T value); }
    static <T,R> R transform(T input,Converter<T,R> converter) {
        return converter.convert(input);
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Integer length=transform("java",new Converter<String,Integer>() {
            public Integer convert(String text) { return text.length(); }
        });
        System.out.println(length);
    }
}
Interview notes and follow-up

Approach: Identify the core data structure or API operation, preserve the required ordering and define how duplicates, missing values and exceptional cases should behave.

Edge cases: Test empty input, one element, duplicate values and boundary conditions where applicable.

Interview follow-up: What makes an interface a functional interface, and can it contain default methods?
